title: Case Study 2: H2S Exposure During Refinery Maintenance — Saudi Arabia
learningObjectives: Understand the specific hazards of H2S and why it is called the 'silent killer'
Identify PTW and gas detection failures that led to a near-fatal exposure
Analyse the role of emergency response readiness in reducing harm severity
Develop corrective actions targeting both equipment and behavioural controls

content.text: H2S (hydrogen sulfide) is detectable by smell at low concentrations but causes olfactory paralysis at higher concentrations — workers can no longer smell it and lose consciousness without warning. Even a brief exposure above 300 ppm can be fatal.

A maintenance technician (Carlos, 42) was assigned to inspect a heat exchanger at a sour gas refinery in Jubail Industrial City, Saudi Arabia. The exchanger had previously processed hydrocarbon streams containing H2S. Carlos was preparing the work area for mechanical isolation when he entered the exchanger bay without wearing his personal H2S gas monitor. He was found unconscious approximately 10 minutes later by a passing instrument technician.

Emergency response was activated. Carlos was rescued with breathing apparatus and taken to the medical centre. He survived but required 3 days of hospital treatment for H2S inhalation and mild pulmonary oedema. The incident was classified as a High Potential Near Fatality.

items: NEVER attempt to rescue an H2S victim without a self-contained breathing apparatus (SCBA) — two additional workers were overcome attempting unprotected rescue in a similar 2019 incident
Activate plant emergency alarm and evacuation for the affected zone
Emergency response team to perform rescue with full SCBA
Provide 100% oxygen to the victim — this is the primary medical treatment for H2S exposure
Stop all work in the exchanger bay area and lock out the hazardous zone
Notify MHRSD (Saudi Ministry of Human Resources) and RCJY (Royal Commission Jubail) within 24 hours
Preserve the scene: do not move the monitor from the tool room, secure the fixed detector unit
Retrieve Carlos's personal H2S monitor from the tool room — document its location and calibration status
Inspect and test the fixed H2S gas detection sensor in the bay — record its calibration history
Collect the issued Permit to Work for the heat exchanger inspection
Gather calibration records and maintenance work orders for the fixed gas detector
Interview the instrument technician who found Carlos, the permit issuer, and Carlos's supervisor
Review the last 6 months of H2S emergency drill records
Check the Job Safety Analysis (JSA) completed for the day's work

content.text: The unsafe acts and conditions that directly caused the exposure.

rows: Personal H2S monitor not worn — left in tool room
Fixed area gas detector faulty for 4 days — silent failure, no alarm triggered
Atmospheric testing not conducted before entering the bay
Buddy system required by company procedure was not followed
Rescue SCBA units stored 150m from the work location — delayed rescue

content.text: The management system failures that allowed the immediate causes to develop.

rows: PTW deficiency — H2S risk not included in the permit risk assessment section
PTW reviewed: chemical hazard box not ticked
Permit issuer not trained to identify H2S risk in maintenance PTWs
Issuer's PTW training certificate: basic level only
Fixed gas detector maintenance deferred — faulty for 4 days, no escalation
Maintenance work order raised day 1, repair scheduled for day 7
No enforcement of buddy system — supervisor assumed workers followed the rule
Buddy system checklist not used in the last 3 weeks
H2S emergency response drills last held 7 months ago
Drill records reviewed — no drills since previous year
JSA completed for the task but did not address atmospheric hazards in the bay
JSA form sighted: hazard column blank for chemical exposures

content.text: The fundamental management system failures that created fertile conditions for this incident.

rows: Safety-critical equipment repairs deprioritised vs production equipment
Maintenance backlog showed 12 safety-critical items overdue vs 2 production items
Culture of tolerance for PPE non-compliance — 'no one ever checks'
Workers disclosed in interviews: personal monitors routinely not worn in the area
PTW quality assurance system absent — no second-check for H2S-rated areas
No requirement in the PTW procedure for a second authorizer in H2S zones
Competency gap — workers not reassessed on H2S hazards after initial induction
No annual H2S refresher training policy existed at the site
No leading indicator monitoring — PTW quality and PPE wear rate not tracked
HSE KPI dashboard did not include any PTW quality metrics
Suspend all work in H2S-rated areas pending audit of all fixed gas detectors
100% personal H2S monitor audit — all worn, calibrated, and functioning
Repair or replace the faulty fixed gas detector
Position rescue SCBA units within 30m of all H2S-rated work areas
Review and re-issue all active PTWs in H2S areas — ensure H2S risk assessed
Train all PTW issuers on H2S hazard identification requirements
Conduct H2S emergency response drill across all shifts
Implement mandatory buddy system log with supervisor sign-off
Add H2S atmospheric testing requirement as mandatory PTW checklist item
Install automatic safety-critical maintenance escalation in CMMS system
Implement annual H2S refresher training for all site personnel
Add PTW quality audit score as monthly HSE KPI

content.text: A faulty gas detection system that is not repaired promptly is not just a maintenance issue — it is a safety-critical failure. Any gas detector fault in an H2S area must be treated as an emergency and escalated immediately. 'We've raised a work order' is not an acceptable response when lives are at risk.

The buddy system exists precisely for situations where a worker becomes incapacitated silently (as H2S causes). When the buddy system is not enforced, the first responders in an H2S incident are often members of the public or passersby — untrained and without SCBA, creating secondary casualties.

NEBOSH IG1 Element 7 connection: This incident relates directly to chemical and biological agents — specifically the recognition, evaluation, and control of atmospheric chemical hazards. NEBOSH exam answers must distinguish between immediate causes (the act/condition) and underlying causes (the system failure), and must recommend controls in hierarchy order: elimination > substitution > engineering controls > administrative controls > PPE.

H2S is endemic to Gulf oil and gas operations — sour crude processing, water injection wells, and wastewater systems all produce H2S. Saudi Aramco's General Instruction GI-0002.102 mandates personal H2S monitors for all personnel entering H2S-rated areas, buddy system compliance, and a maximum response time for rescue teams of 5 minutes. Qatar Energy and ADNOC have equivalent requirements. HSE engineers working in Gulf O&G must be fully familiar with OSHA 1910.1000 (air contaminants), ANSI Z88.2 (respiratory protection), and the company-specific H2S contingency plan.
